What did P.L. 2024, c.39 change for owners?

The law was approved July 10, 2024 and covers any lien not yet foreclosed on that date. Its biggest change protects equity. In a foreclosure on a tax sale certificate, the owner or heirs may demand in writing, before final judgment, that the holder go through a judicial sale or a sheriff's internet auction, the way a mortgage is foreclosed. If no demand is made, the holder can foreclose without a sale and the owner has no claim for equity.

  • The summons and complaint must carry a bold notice of this right.
  • The sheriff pays surplus funds to the Superior Court clerk, and the owner applies for them by motion.
  • A holder that is not a municipality must give 30 days' written notice by certified mail before filing, or it cannot recover search and counsel fees.
  • Once a foreclosure complaint is filed, attorney's fees of $2,500 are added to the redemption amount, plus listed costs and a title search fee capped at $350.
  • If the owner asked for a sale, the holder takes a first lien of 10 percent of the surplus for administrative costs, up to $5,000.

How should a New Jersey owner handle a tax lien when selling the house?

Start by asking the tax collector which certificates exist and which charges remain unpaid. A buyer will expect clear title, and a redemption that includes foreclosure costs costs more than one made early. If a complaint has been filed, redemption must be made in that case, and the court can set attorney's fees and costs at any point.

A sale also gives you a way to protect equity. An owner who sells for market value and pays the redemption amount from proceeds keeps the remainder. Waiting through a foreclosure without demanding a sale can mean losing that equity. Legal Services of New Jersey runs a statewide hotline at 1-888-LSNJ-LAW for owners who cannot afford a lawyer, and Branchburg's tax office points readers to the same number.

Frequently asked questions

What is a tax sale certificate in New Jersey?

It is a lien sold at auction for unpaid taxes or municipal charges. The buyer does not receive the deed, but may earn interest and can foreclose if the owner never redeems.

How long do New Jersey owners have to redeem before foreclosure?

Two years when an investor holds the certificate, and six months when the municipality does. Redemption stays open until the Superior Court enters a final judgment barring it.

Can a New Jersey owner lose a house over a small tax debt?

Yes, if the certificate goes unredeemed and the holder completes a foreclosure. The 2024 law lets the owner demand a judicial sale or sheriff internet auction before final judgment to preserve equity.

Do fees get added to a tax lien in New Jersey?

Yes. After a foreclosure complaint, the redemption amount includes $2,500 in attorney's fees and listed costs, with a search fee capped at $350. Earlier notice costs are smaller.

Who do I call to get a redemption figure?

Call the municipal tax collector in the town where the house sits. Ask for a written payoff good through your planned closing date.

What closing costs does a New Jersey seller pay?

Expect one state fee, one possible state surcharge and a handful of private costs. The Realty Transfer Fee lands on the seller at recording, while the buyer carries none of it, and the Division confirms that no sales tax applies to a home sale. Private costs come from your contract and lender, and they vary by deal.

  • The Realty Transfer Fee, a rate times the price shown in the deed.
  • A graduated percent fee when the price tops $1,000,000.
  • Broker compensation, whatever your written agreement says.
  • An estimated income tax deposit if you live outside New Jersey and no exemption fits.
  • The mortgage payoff and any property tax still owed.

Most sellers also supply form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller. A deed that claims any exemption must carry that affidavit (NJ Division of Taxation).

How is the New Jersey Realty Transfer Fee calculated?

The charge is stacked in slices, with a dollar amount for each $500 and a higher rate for each higher slice of the price. It starts from the price stated in the deed. In a few situations the Division substitutes assessed value divided by the Director's Ratio. Every deed that conveys title is covered unless an exemption fits.

Fee schedule for a standard sale priced above $350,000 (Division of Taxation)
Slice of the priceRate per $500
$0 to $150,000$2.90
$150,000 to $200,000$4.25
$200,000 to $550,000$4.80
$550,000 to $850,000$5.30
$850,000 to $1,000,000$5.80
Above $1,000,000$6.05

A cheaper schedule governs any sale at $350,000 or below, starting at $2.00 per $500 and topping out at $3.90. Stacking those slices on a $325,000 sale yields $1,910, the same answer the Division's FAQ gives. Stacking the table above on a $600,000 sale gives 870, 425, 3,360 and 530, a total of $5,185.

Qualifying seniors, blind or disabled persons and low and moderate income housing use reduced rates. The senior and disability reduction belongs to the person, so an estate or trust cannot claim it.

How does the percent fee on sales above $1 million work?

It is a percentage of the full sale price that the seller owes when consideration passes $1,000,000. Since P.L. 2025, c. 69 took effect on July 10, 2025, the fee is charged to the grantor instead of the buyer. Older descriptions that call it a 1 percent buyer's mansion tax are out of date for deeds submitted on or after that date.

  • 1% of total consideration when the price runs from $1,000,000 up to $2,000,000.
  • 2% when it runs above $2,000,000 up to $2,500,000.
  • 2.5% above $2,500,000 up to $3,000,000.
  • 3% above $3,000,000 up to $3,500,000.
  • 3.5% on prices above $3,500,000.

Each rate is applied to the entire price, so the cost jumps at each threshold instead of building slice by slice. A seller close to a threshold, such as $2,000,000 or $2,500,000, should ask the closing attorney for the exact figure before accepting an offer. The Division's memo works a $2.75 million deed at 2.5 percent, or $68,750 due at recording. It covers Class 2 residential property, farms with a residential building, Class 4A commercial property and cooperative units. A limited refund window applied to deeds above $2 million with contracts fully signed before July 10, 2025 and recorded by November 15, 2025, and that date has passed (Division memo).

Which deeds escape the transfer fee entirely?

The Division lists a long set of full exemptions, and the seller claims one on form RTF-1. Check the facts carefully, because the Division reads each exemption narrowly.

  • Husband and wife, or parent and child, with adopted children counted and stepchildren left out.
  • An executor or administrator passing the house to a named devisee or legal heir.
  • Deeds for consideration under $100.
  • A deed whose only job is to confirm or fix one already on record.
  • Tax sale deeds and deeds on partition.
  • A deed between the divorced spouses filed within 90 days after the decree.

Some transfers look exempt and are not. A sale by an executor to someone who is not named in the will pays the fee. A will that orders a sale and a split of the cash is treated as a gift of money. Moving a house into a trust for other beneficiaries is taxable, and terms of a divorce settlement agreement do not count as specific performance of a judgment. At a sheriff's sale, form RTF-8 is also required, and it is no exemption.

Who sets broker compensation in New Jersey?

You and your brokerage do, in writing. Under P.L. 2024, c. 32, effective August 1, 2024, the brokerage must sign a brokerage services agreement with the seller in every residential transaction. That agreement states the term, the amount of compensation and how it is calculated, and it must say that compensation is fully negotiable and not set by law (DOBI Bulletin 24-11).

  • Compensation may be a flat fee, a percentage of the price or another lawful method.
  • It can be paid by the seller, the buyer, a third party, or shared between brokerages.
  • The agreement must show whether the agency is exclusive or non-exclusive.
  • The brokerage must obtain a signed property condition disclosure statement from the seller.

Showings also changed. At a residential showing open to the public, agents must post a sign saying the agent represents the seller and that what a visitor tells the agent is not confidential. If you hold your own open house through a brokerage, expect that sign at the door. Read the agency section before you sign. New Jersey law now recognizes seller's agents, buyer's agents, disclosed dual agents, designated agents and transaction brokers, and each owes you different duties.

Where is the deed recorded, and what if it lands in the wrong county?

A deed is recorded by the clerk of the county containing the parcel. The package includes the RTF paperwork and a GIT/REP form, which the Division describes as two separate requirements handed in at closing. Acceptance is the clerk's decision.

If the package went to the wrong county, record it again in the right one. Form RTF-3 recovers the state share, and the county share needs a separate request to the office that took it by mistake. Have your title agent confirm the county before anything is mailed.

What do two sample New Jersey sales look like in dollars?

Stacking the slices from the schedule makes the numbers concrete. A $450,000 sale pays 870 on the first $150,000, 425 on the next $50,000 and 2,400 on the last $250,000, which totals $3,695 in Realty Transfer Fee. No percent fee applies, because the price stays under $1,000,000.

A $1,200,000 sale shows how the pieces add up. Stacking the fee slices gives 870, 425, 3,360, 3,180, 1,740 and 2,420, or $11,995. The percent fee at the 1 percent tier is $12,000 on the full price, so the two state charges together reach $23,995 before commission, attorney fees or a payoff. These totals come straight from the Division's rate tables and are not a quote for any deal.

A seller living outside New Jersey also faces the estimated tax deposit described on our capital gains page, and that deposit is credited on the later tax return.

Frequently asked questions

Which side of the table owes the transfer fee?

The seller does. Collection happens at recording, and a buyer on an ordinary purchase owes none of it.

Does a house sale carry sales tax?

No, the Division of Taxation says home sales are outside sales tax.

What does the fee run on a $325,000 sale?

It runs $1,910 with no exemption, the figure the Division's FAQ gives for that price.

Does the old mansion tax still fall on buyers?

For deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025, the seller is responsible for the graduated percent fee on prices above $1,000,000. The rate starts at 1 percent and climbs to 3.5 percent.

Can I negotiate the real estate commission in New Jersey?

Yes. Broker compensation is fully negotiable, not set by law, and must appear in the brokerage services agreement.

Who handles probate in New Jersey?

Each of New Jersey's 21 counties has a Surrogate's Court, and the surrogate of the county where the person lived handles the estate paperwork. The New Jersey Judiciary publishes a directory of county surrogates with the street address and phone number of every office, from Atlantic and Bergen through Union and Warren. The directory was updated on September 8, 2026.

The person who runs the estate is the executor named in a will or, when there is no will, an administrator. That legal representative is the one the Division of Taxation expects to file the inheritance tax return and ask for the waivers that release bank accounts and real estate. Anyone who inherits a house in New Jersey should call the surrogate's office first, because the office can say which papers are needed for a will, which for an intestate estate, and what fees apply.

Can a small New Jersey estate skip formal administration?

Sometimes, but the dollar limits are low and they include real estate. Under N.J.S.A. 3B:10-3, as amended by P.L. 2015, c. 232, a surviving spouse, civil union partner or domestic partner can take an intestate estate without administration when the total real and personal assets do not exceed $50,000. The survivor signs an affidavit before the county surrogate, and the first $10,000 of the estate is free from the decedent's debts.

Where there is no surviving spouse or partner, N.J.S.A. 3B:10-4 lets one heir collect the assets of an intestate estate worth no more than $20,000 after getting the written consent of the other heirs and signing an affidavit with the surrogate. Both rules count real property. A house in most New Jersey towns is worth far more than these limits, so a home sale almost always goes through a full appointment as executor or administrator.

What does New Jersey's inheritance tax mean for an inherited house?

New Jersey charges a transfer inheritance tax that depends on who receives the property, and it can hold up a sale. The Division of Taxation explains that the law freezes New Jersey financial and real estate assets in the decedent's name until any inheritance tax is assessed and paid. The return and payment are due within eight months of the date of death.

Beneficiaries fall into four classes, and the class sets the rate:

New Jersey inheritance tax classes
ClassWho is includedTax
ASpouse, civil union or domestic partner, children, grandchildren, parents, grandparents, stepchildrenExempt
CSiblings, sons-in-law and daughters-in-law11% to 16% after a $25,000 exemption per beneficiary
DNieces, nephews, cousins, friends, ex-spouses, uncertified partners15% on the first $700,000, then 16%
ECharitable institutionsExempt

Source: Division of Taxation, IT-R instructions and A Guide to Being an Executor.

A full return is required whenever anything passes to a Class C, D or E beneficiary, a mutually acknowledged child or a trust. Unpaid tax draws 10 percent annual interest, and asking for more time to file does not move the payment date.

How does an executor get permission to transfer or sell the property?

Real estate cannot move out of the decedent's name without a tax waiver from the state. The Division's executor guide says Form 0-1 is issued only by the Division of Taxation, it is not on the website for download, and real estate transfers always require it. When every beneficiary is exempt and no tax is owed, the executor files a Form L-9 affidavit with the Inheritance and Estate Tax Branch to receive the 0-1 for real estate.

Other points the guide and instructions make:

  • Form L-8, a self-executing waiver, works for bank accounts only when no inheritance or estate tax is due and nothing is filed with the state
  • banks may release up to 50 percent of the funds on hand to the executor, administrator or a joint owner before a waiver arrives
  • property that a spouse or civil union partner holds as tenants by the entirety, and passes to the survivor, needs no waiver and is not reported
  • assets should be reported at their fair market value on the date of death, not on the filing date

Allow time. The guide says to plan for several months of processing after a return is filed, and about 40 to 50 percent of returns are audited, which adds more months. The Inheritance and Estate Tax Hotline is 609-292-5033, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Does New Jersey still have an estate tax?

Not for recent deaths. According to the Division's executor guide, the estate tax return requirement depends on the year of death: the exemption was $675,000 for 2016 and earlier, $2 million for 2017, and for deaths in 2018 or after every estate is exempt and no estate tax return is needed. The inheritance tax is a separate tax and still applies to Class C and D beneficiaries.

An estate never pays more than the higher of the two state taxes, so executors check both. Federal estate tax is a different matter and is not handled by the state branch.

Is the sale of an inherited New Jersey house exempt from the realty transfer fee?

It depends on who the buyer is. The Division's transfer fee FAQ says a transfer by an executor to the devisees or heirs named in the will or the intestacy law is exempt. A sale by the executor to anyone else is not exempt. A will that directs a house to be sold and the money divided among children does not change this, because bequests of sale money are treated as gifts of money rather than devises of land.

The senior, blind or disabled partial exemption is personal and cannot be given to a decedent or an estate. A sale to an outside buyer therefore carries the fee. Ask the county clerk or the title agent for the fee figure before you set a net price.

What steps help an heir sell a house during probate?

The order of tasks matters more than the speed of any one task. A New Jersey heir can keep the sale moving by doing these things early:

  • obtain the death certificate and the original will, and ask the county surrogate how to qualify as executor or administrator
  • list every beneficiary and work out its tax class to learn whether a full return is required
  • file the L-9 or the IT-R, depending on the class, and request the Form 0-1 for the house
  • keep property taxes, insurance and utilities current while the waiver is pending
  • choose a buyer who can close once the waiver issues and the representative holds court-issued authority

A buyer who pays cash and accepts the house as is can shorten the repair and financing steps, but the waiver and the surrogate's appointment still control the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell a house I inherited in New Jersey?

In most cases yes. A house usually exceeds the $50,000 and $20,000 small-estate limits, and real estate transfers always need a Form 0-1 waiver from the Division of Taxation. A surviving spouse who holds the home as tenants by the entirety is the main exception.

How long do I have to file the New Jersey inheritance tax return?

Eight months from the date of death. The Division publishes a chart that matches each month of death to the same date eight months later, and when that date does not exist the due date is the first day of the following month. Unpaid tax carries 10 percent annual interest.

Do children pay inheritance tax on a parent's house in New Jersey?

No. Children, grandchildren, parents and spouses are Class A beneficiaries and are exempt. Siblings are Class C and pay 11 percent to 16 percent after a $25,000 exemption, while nieces, nephews and friends are Class D at 15 percent to 16 percent.

Can a bank release money before the waiver arrives?

Partly. Banks and financial institutions may release up to 50 percent of the funds on hand to the executor, administrator or a joint account owner before a waiver is received. They must also pay checks written to New Jersey Inheritance and Estate Tax from the account.

Is there a New Jersey estate tax on a death in 2026?

No. The state's executor guide shows that for deaths in 2018 or after, all estates are exempt and no estate tax return is required. Inheritance tax may still apply to Class C and D beneficiaries.

A New Jersey seller of a home must complete a property condition disclosure statement, known as the PCDS, and it must be signed. The form comes from the Division of Consumer Affairs under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-29.1(d), and the statute behind it is N.J.S.A. 56:8-19.1. P.L. 2024, c.32 made it a duty for real estate brokerage firms to obtain the signed statement from a residential seller.

A seller without an agent has the same job. The law says that a seller who is not working with a brokerage firm, or who works with a firm acting as transaction broker, must hand the statement to the buyer before the buyer becomes obligated under any contract. That timing matters. A statement delivered after the contract is signed does not meet the rule as written in section 2(e) of P.L. 2024, c.32.

Does New Jersey require a flood disclosure?

Yes. Since March 20, 2024, every seller of real property in the state must disclose flood risk information through the PCDS before the buyer is bound by a purchase contract. The Department of Environmental Protection explains two parts. The seller states whether the property is in FEMA's Special Flood Hazard Area or Moderate Flood Hazard Area, and the seller reports any actual knowledge about the property's flood risks.

The law is P.L. 2023, c.94, enacted July 3, 2023. The same page notes that sea-level rise is expected to meet or exceed 2.1 feet above 2000 levels by 2050 and that heavier rainfall raises flash flood risk inland. DEP offers a Flood Risk Notification Tool to help sellers find the zone answers. Because the duty applies to every seller, a cash sale or an as-is sale does not remove the question.

Which other New Jersey disclosures show up when you sell a house?

The Department of Banking and Insurance publishes a consumer guide that lists the items beyond the statement. Several belong to the seller, and others are mostly for the buyer to investigate.

  • Lead paint: for a house built before 1978, the seller must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, give the buyer a lead disclosure form, and share any records or reports.
  • Material physical conditions: P.L. 2024, c.32 requires the listing brokerage to disclose existing material information about the property's physical condition that it knows or that a reasonable effort would reveal.
  • Stigmatized property: a seller and agent do not have to volunteer a haunting or a violent death, but must answer truthfully if the buyer asks.
  • Off-site conditions: municipal clerks keep lists of nearby conditions that may affect value, and buyers can review them.
  • Megan's Law: the county prosecutor decides how notice is given about convicted offenders in an area.

Mold, radon and asbestos appear in the same guide as inspection topics for the buyer, so expect questions about them during an inspection even though they are not separate seller forms.

What changed when P.L. 2024, c.32 took effect?

The law was signed July 10, 2024 and became effective August 1, 2024. The Real Estate Commission's Bulletin 24-11 explains that it adds designated agency as a fifth business relationship and requires a written brokerage services agreement in residential deals. Compensation terms in that agreement must say expressly that broker pay is negotiable and not set by law.

The Act also requires a posted sign at residential open houses warning visitors that the agent represents the seller and that information given to the agent is not confidential. A seller who lists with an agent should expect to sign the agency disclosure at the start and to hand over the PCDS soon after.

When can a New Jersey buyer or seller walk away after signing?

The Banking and Insurance guide describes an attorney review clause. When a licensee prepares the contract of sale, it must give buyer and seller three business days from delivery of the fully signed contract to consult an attorney. In that period the attorney can propose revisions or cancel the contract. If you hired an attorney to draft the contract instead, the guide says the review period may or may not be included, so ask the attorney.

This is where disclosure answers get tested. A statement that mentions flooding, a past repair or a lead history can lead the buyer's lawyer to ask for a repair credit or a price change during the review days. Answering fully at the start keeps those three days from becoming a renegotiation of surprises.

What happens after the buyer's inspection in New Jersey?

The state's buyer guide recommends an independent home inspection soon after a contract becomes binding, with the buyer present. The inspector reports on the structure, construction and mechanical systems and flags defects or items to replace. If the report shows problems, buyer and seller are held to the time limits written in the contract for delivering the report and for the seller to decide whether to correct the items.

For a seller, the practical point is to read those inspection and response deadlines before signing. Missing the contract's response window can leave you without a say in how a repair issue gets resolved. The guide tells buyers to consult an agent or attorney for the specifics of their contract, and sellers can do the same.

What seller taxes and forms come at a New Jersey closing?

The seller pays the Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. The Division of Taxation calculates it from the consideration in the deed, using a rate per $500 that rises with price. For a deal of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 from $200,000 to $350,000. An Affidavit of Consideration, Form RTF-1, claims any exemption. Sales above $1,000,000 also carry a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent of consideration.

A GIT/REP form is also recorded with the deed. New Jersey resident individuals, estates and trusts sign the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax unless an assurance on that form applies, and the payment cannot be less than 2 percent of the total consideration in the deed. Executors and trustees complete the form for the estate or trust.

Can a seller in foreclosure still sell the house?

Yes. The NJ Courts say the Notice of Intent to Foreclose must state that the debtor can sell or transfer the title. After a sheriff sale the owner also has 10 days to redeem by buying back or selling. Disclosure rules still apply to a distressed sale, so the PCDS, flood answers and any lead form go to the buyer the same way.

The Judiciary also warns about foreclosure rescue and loan modification scams and recommends a free HUD and NJHMFA certified housing counselor. Anyone who asks for an upfront fee to save a home deserves a second look before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Is the property condition disclosure statement required for every New Jersey home sale?

For residential sales, yes. A licensee must obtain the signed statement from the seller, and a seller without an agent must give it to the buyer before the buyer is bound by the contract.

Do I have to disclose that my New Jersey house floods?

Yes, to the extent you know. Every seller must state whether the property is in a FEMA Special or Moderate Flood Hazard Area and report actual knowledge of flood risk before the buyer is obligated.

Is lead paint disclosure required in New Jersey?

Yes for houses built before 1978. The seller discloses known lead-based paint and hazards, provides the lead disclosure form and passes along any records or reports in hand.

Must a New Jersey seller disclose a death in the house?

Not unless asked. Stigmatized property, such as a violent death, does not have to be volunteered, but a seller or agent who knows the answer must give it truthfully when a buyer asks.

Who pays the realty transfer fee in New Jersey?

The seller pays it. The Division of Taxation sets rates per $500 of consideration, and the fee is collected when the deed is recorded with the county clerk.
